title: Design a B-Tree
statement_md:
A **B-tree** keeps a sorted index shallow by making every node wide. A binary
search tree branches two ways per node and needs about `log2(n)` levels; a B-tree
node holds many keys and branches many ways, so it needs about `log_t(n)`. That is
why it is the structure behind essentially every database index and filesystem
directory — each level costs one block read, and there are very few levels.

This problem uses the **minimum degree** formulation. For a tree with minimum
degree `t`:

- Every node holds at most `2t - 1` keys, kept in sorted order.
- Every node except the root holds at least `t - 1` keys.
- An internal node holding `k` keys has exactly `k + 1` children, and its keys are
  separators: everything in child `i` is less than `keys[i]`, and everything in
  child `i + 1` is greater.
- **Every leaf sits at the same depth.** A B-tree never grows downward in one
  spot; it grows only by splitting a full root, which lifts the whole tree by one
  level at once.

Implement the `BTree` class:

- `BTree(t)` initializes an empty tree with minimum degree `t`.
- `insert(key)` inserts `key` and returns `true`. If `key` is already in the tree,
  the tree is left **completely unchanged** — nothing is split — and it returns
  `false`.
- `search(key)` returns `true` if `key` is in the tree.
- `height()` returns the number of levels — `0` for an empty tree, `1` while the
  root is still a leaf.
- `serialize()` returns the key arrays of every node in level order: entry `0` is
  the root's keys, then its children left to right, then their children, and so
  on. An empty tree returns `[]`.

Because `serialize()` exposes the exact shape, the insertion algorithm below is
**part of the specification**, not an implementation detail. A tree that satisfies
every invariant above but was built by splitting at different moments is a wrong
answer here.

**Insertion splits proactively.** Walk down from the root toward the leaf where
`key` belongs, and split any full node *before* stepping into it — rather than
inserting first and splitting on the way back up once a node overflows:

1. If the root holds `2t - 1` keys, split it before descending: make a new root
   whose only child is the old root, then split that child. This is the only way
   the height ever increases.
2. At each internal node, find the child `key` belongs in. If that child holds
   `2t - 1` keys, split it, then compare `key` against the separator that just
   moved up to decide which of the two halves to descend into.
3. On reaching a leaf, insert `key` into its sorted key array.

**Splitting a full child** whose keys are `k[0] … k[2t-2]`: the key at index
`t - 1` moves up into the parent, `k[0] … k[t-2]` stay in the left node, and
`k[t] … k[2t-2]` move into a new right node placed immediately after the left one.
An internal node's first `t` children stay left and its last `t` move right. Both
halves end up holding exactly `t - 1` keys, the minimum a non-root node may
hold — which is why it has to be the median that moves up.

Splitting before the descent is what keeps this simple: the parent is guaranteed
to have room for the key coming up, so a split never cascades and you never have
to walk back toward the root.
constraints: At most $10^4$ calls total will be made to `insert`, `search`, `height`, and `serialize`.
Keys are unique — `insert` on a key already in the tree leaves it unchanged.

solutions.title: Approach 1: Recursive, Splitting Full Nodes on the Way Down
solutions.intuition_md:
The whole difficulty of inserting into a B-tree is that a node can overflow, and
fixing an overflow means pushing a key up into the parent — which may itself
overflow, and so on toward the root. Handling that cascade is fiddly, and it is
the part most implementations get wrong.

CLRS removes the cascade entirely with one change of timing: split full nodes on
the way *down*, before you know whether you will even need the room. By the time
you reach the leaf, every node on the path has at most `2t - 2` keys, so the leaf
has space and so does every parent that might receive a promoted key. A split can
never trigger another split, because the node it pushes into was already made
non-full a moment ago.

The trade is that you sometimes split a node you did not have to. That costs a
little space (nodes sit half-empty more often) and buys an algorithm with no
upward phase at all — one pass, one direction.
solutions.algorithm_md:
Each node stores just `keys` (sorted) and `children` (empty for a leaf, so a
separate leaf flag is unnecessary).

`_slot(node, key)` scans the node's keys for the first one not less than `key`.
That single index answers both questions asked of a node: if `keys[i] == key` the
search is done, and otherwise `children[i]` is the subtree to descend into.

`_split_child(parent, i)` does the surgery described in the statement — move
`keys[t-1]` up into `parent.keys[i]`, keep `keys[:t-1]` in the full node, move
`keys[t:]` into a fresh right sibling inserted at `children[i+1]`, and split the
children `[:t]` / `[t:]` when the node is internal.

- `insert` first calls `search`. A key already present must leave the tree
  untouched, and the descent splits as it goes, so the membership test has to
  happen before any of that.
- Then the root is checked: if it is full, a new root is created above it and
  split, which is the only place the tree gets taller.
- `_insert_nonfull` recurses on the invariant its name states — the node it is
  handed always has room. It splits the child it is about to enter if that child
  is full, re-compares `key` against the newly promoted separator to pick a half,
  and recurses. At a leaf it just inserts into the sorted array.
- `height` walks the leftmost spine, which is valid precisely because all leaves
  are at the same depth; `serialize` is an ordinary BFS.
solutions.time_complexity: O(t\log_t n)\text{ per insert/search, } O(n)\text{ for serialize}
solutions.time_complexity_reason: The tree has about log_t(n) levels and each level costs one linear scan of a node's keys, which is O(t). Splitting is O(t) too, and proactive splitting does at most one per level, so it does not change the bound. serialize visits every node.
solutions.space_complexity_reason: Keys are stored once. The recursion is only as deep as the tree, which is tiny — even t = 2 over a million keys is about 20 frames.

solutions.title: Approach 2: Iterative, with Binary Search Inside Each Node
solutions.intuition_md:
Proactive splitting has a consequence that is easy to miss: because every node on
the path was made non-full before you entered it, you never need to go back up.
And if you never go back up, you do not need the recursion stack — or a parent
stack, or parent pointers. The parent is simply the node you are standing on when
you decide to split its child.

So the same algorithm rewrites into a plain `while` loop over the path. That is
worth seeing, because it makes the structural claim concrete: the reason a
top-down B-tree insert can be written iteratively without any bookkeeping is
exactly the reason splits do not cascade.

The second change is inside the node. A B-tree node is wide on purpose — that is
the entire point of the structure — so the linear scan Approach 1 uses to find a
key's slot costs `O(t)` per level, and `t` is not small. The keys are already
sorted, so `bisect` finds the slot in `O(log t)` instead.
solutions.algorithm_md:
`search` and the descent both use `bisect.bisect_left(node.keys, key)`, which
returns the index of the first key not less than `key` — the same index Approach
1's linear scan computes, so the two agree on shape by construction.

`insert` is one loop:

- Reject a duplicate up front, then split the root if it is full, exactly as
  before.
- While the current node has children: pick the slot with `bisect_left`, split
  that child if it is full, nudge the slot right when `key` is greater than the
  separator that just arrived, and step into the child. No stack, no recursion —
  the parent is only ever needed at the instant its child is split, and it is
  right there.
- At the leaf, `bisect.insort` places the key.

`_split_child`, `height` and `serialize` are unchanged; the shape a tree ends up
with depends only on when nodes are split, not on how the path was walked.
solutions.time_complexity: O(\log t\log_t n)\text{ per insert/search, } O(n)\text{ for serialize}
solutions.time_complexity_reason: Same number of levels, but bisect finds the slot in a node in O(log t) instead of O(t). That factor is invisible at t = 2 and matters exactly where B-trees are actually used, with nodes sized to a disk block and t in the hundreds.
solutions.space_complexity_reason: Because a node is split before it is entered, the descent never needs to revisit a parent, so no stack of any kind is required — not recursion, not parent pointers. That is a property of proactive splitting, not of the loop.
